about: Golden cases for M1, meetings from mail. Every name, address and exchange is invented. `body` is the conversation note as the pass reads it (`### Sender — sent`, then the email). `expect` is what a person reading the emails would put on the agenda, one line per meeting: `fixed <start stamp>` or `cancelled <day>`, plus ` @ <place>` when the place matters. `oracle` is an answer a perfect model would give, written by hand: replaying it through `meetings::parse` and `meetings::resolve` must give `expect`, which is what the CI test checks. `recorded` holds real models' answers from live runs (`tests/eval_meetings.rs`). `here`, when present, is the reader's own clock (a zone name or offset): a time the emails put on another clock must come out on this one (2026-10-23). A heading may carry its offset (`### Sender — 2026-10-07 22:30 -05:00`, formicaria 0.20): it is read onto `here` as the pass reads it, and a day the email names ("tomorrow") is counted from the sender's own day (2026-10-24).

### Tom Reyes — 2026-09-30 10:00

Dear Ana,

let us meet on Thursday 2 October at 2:30pm in room B12 to plan the project.

Tom

### Ana Ruiz — 2026-09-30 18:00

Dear Tom,

Thursday at 2:30pm in B12 works for me.

Ana

### Tom Reyes — 2026-10-03 09:00

Thanks for today. Next meeting: Friday 10 October at 4pm, same room.

### Ana Ruiz — 2026-10-03 12:00

Noted, see you on Friday.

### Tom Reyes — 2026-10-10 17:00

Good progress today. We meet again on Friday 17 October at 4pm online: https://meet.example.org/j/4821

### Ana Ruiz — 2026-10-16 20:00

Dear Tom,

could we start at 4:30pm instead? I have a lab until 4.

Ana

### Tom Reyes — 2026-10-17 08:00

Yes, Friday 17 October at 4:30pm is fine, same link.

### Tom Reyes — 2026-10-23 09:28

Dear Ana,

as discussed in person, for the next weeks:

- a presentation for next time, close to the one you will give at the end of the term: the problem, what is known, what you built and what is still open. Keep it to twelve slides and leave time for questions.
- a simple but realistic simulation of a person doing a task. For instance, a robot with several objects on a table that watches a person sitting in front of the computer and listens to what they say. The person may not know which objects are on the table, and may change their mind halfway through.
- the robot should keep a belief over what the person wants and update it with every word and every glance, and it should say so when it is unsure rather than guess.
- a short written section on the related work: the three groups we talked about, what each assumes about the person, and where your approach differs. Two pages are enough.
- the data you already recorded, cleaned, with a note on what was thrown away and why. If some sessions are unusable, say how many and what went wrong, so that we can avoid it next time.
- a first evaluation, even a rough one: how often the robot picks the right object, how early it is right, and how often it asks. Compare it with the simple baseline that always waits for the full sentence.
- a list of the questions you could not answer on your own, so that we spend the meeting on those and not on what is already clear.

On the practical side, please put the code in the shared repository with a short README that says how to run the simulation from scratch on a fresh machine, which versions you used, and where the recorded data lives. Try it once yourself on another computer before the meeting, so that we do not lose time on installation problems.

If any of this is too much for one week, tell me which parts you would rather move to the week after, and we will plan around it. It is better to have two parts done well than five parts half done.

Best,
Tom

### Tom Reyes — 2026-10-23 09:30

I suggest the next meeting on Monday 2nd of Nov 16:30 Tokyo time, let me know if it works for you.

Tom Reyes is inviting you to a scheduled meeting.
